content_html:
Moss forms a thicker mat than algae and often anchors itself in joints, pores, and shaded areas. Mechanical removal is usually the first step, but recurrence depends mainly on how long the patio stays damp.

Lift moss without damaging the patio surface

Use a blunt scraper or a stiff brush that is safe for the finish, working along joints rather than gouging across them. On softer or weathered surfaces, excessive pressure can remove aggregate, sealer, or fibers.

Clean away the debris after loosening it

Collect loosened material before rinsing so it is not pushed into drains or joints. If you use a moss-control product, follow the label and confirm it is suitable for the paving and nearby plants.

Avoid extreme pressure on joints or soft stone

A pressure washer can speed up the job on some surfaces, but it can also blow sand from joints, etch stone, or raise wood grain. Start with the lowest effective pressure and increase only if the material tolerates it.

Change the conditions that keep the patio wet

Dense shade, downspouts that discharge nearby, and persistent puddles all favor moss. Correcting those conditions usually reduces recurrence more effectively than repeating treatments every few weeks.
